title: Shohei Ohtani, still facing uncertain pitching timeline, says biceps is also an issue
content:
LOS ANGELES — Shohei Ohtani’s timeline to return to a big-league mound remains the biggest unknown for the back-to-back champion Los Angeles Dodgers ahead of MLB’s Aug. 3 trade deadline. That picture did not get any clearer Tuesday, when Ohtani said his health concerns go beyond just his left knee.

Ohtani said he is still recovering from the right biceps discomfort that earlier this month caused him to be removed early from a game and miss another one entirely. It was the first time the Dodgers star had taken questions since since July 10.

“My biceps (is) not 100 percent,” Ohtani said through interpreter Will Ireton. “Just similar issue with the knee. Do we consider pushing this? It is still July. So I think the conversation would be a little different if we’re in August or September.”

The four-time MVP has not pitched in a game since July 3, and has not thrown off a mound since a 31-pitch bullpen session in Philadelphia last Wednesday. He was slated to throw another bullpen session on Saturday in New York, but those plans were scrapped when his knee and biceps did not feel 100 percent.

“If I was completely, no issue, 100 percent, I think things would have gone the way it was supposed to,” Ohtani said. “But if I’m at 90 percent, which means 10 percent not quite there, then there’s not really a necessity to force the issue.”

The Dodgers have shut down Ohtani from throwing outside of some plyo balls. Manager Dave Roberts did not have a timeline for when Ohtani would throw his next bullpen session. How long it takes for Ohtani to feel 100 percent remains to be seen.

Ohtani continues to be in Roberts’ everyday lineup as a designated hitter, which he has said does not affect the knee. Ohtani entered Tuesday with a .711 OPS in July, his worst month offensively since August 2020 (.695). Ohtani led off Tuesday’s 7-6 loss to the Seattle Mariners with a solo home run off Luis Castillo, but had been 7-for-38 (.184) since receiving an injection to treat his balky left knee during the All-Star break.

Roberts said there are no plans to give Ohtani a few days to let his body catch up.

“Until I hear otherwise, he’s going to be in the lineup,” Roberts said.

The Dodgers still feel Ohtani serves them more in the lineup right now than in the rotation. They also do not want Ohtani pitching with a compromised knee for fear that doing so would risk a more serious arm injury. The more time Ohtani misses, however, the more he will need to build back up.

“You’re looking at over three weeks (without pitching) right now, so there has to be a bill,” Roberts said. “So I just don’t know. I don’t think anyone can kind of foresee what that looks like.”

Ohtani’s status is not expected to alter the Dodgers’ plans prior to Monday’s trade deadline, even as other clubs are expected to enter the bidding for Detroit Tigers ace Tarik Skubal. The organization is still confident Ohtani will pitch again this season, even if there is no clear timeline.

“Given where we’re at in the calendar, if the knee continues to get better, the arm continues to feel better, I would expect him to pitch,” Roberts said.

When Ohtani’s ready, the Dodgers can use last year as a template.

The Dodgers ramped up Ohtani in 2025 following his return from a second major elbow surgery, essentially treating those starts as rehab outings while Ohtani did not count toward the Dodgers’ 13-pitcher limit as a two-way player. He can return to the rotation even while not fully built up, opening games with one or two innings and essentially progressing with each outing.

Meanwhile, reinforcements are on the way. Blake Snell, who is recovering from surgery to remove loose bodies in his elbow, is expected to make a four-inning rehab start with Class-A Ontario on Wednesday in what could be his final step before a potential return. Tyler Glasnow will also take the mound Wednesday at Dodger Stadium for his second live session against hitters before a potential rehab assignment of his own after missing multiple months with back spasms.

“I feel very confident,” Roberts said. “Obviously with Snell being more built up, everything that I’m hearing from the medical staff. I think Tyler is in a really good spot physically, on his way back to going out. And then Shohei, I just think that we’re trying to be prudent. So overall, in total, I feel very good for the rest with all three of these guys as starting pitchers.”

The Dodgers are also cautiously optimistic that Gavin Stone could start a rehab assignment soon after missing all of 2025 this season thus far after shoulder surgery.

Beyond the rotation, there was more positive news for the Dodgers.

Kiké Hernández made his return from the injured list Tuesday, using a hyperbaric chamber and stem-cell injection as part of a rehab program that got him back well ahead of schedule on a Grade 3 oblique strain. Hernández said he initially feared the injury had cost him the season, which triggered a panic attack. He was left constipated for six days, he said.

“Sitting in traffic, I had to call my wife, and I could barely talk,” Hernández said. “But I was like, “Look, this is what happened. I don’t know what’s going on with my body. Maybe I’m too old.”

Closer Edwin Díaz, the club’s prized signing last winter, is expected back Wednesday after undergoing surgery to remove bone chips from his elbow.

Franchise catcher Will Smith is also finally pain-free and resuming baseball activities, Roberts said. Smith has been out since June 5 with an inflamed disc in his neck and has missed enough time that the Dodgers have at least explored potentially upgrading their backup catcher spot behind Dalton Rushing until Smith returns.

“It’s certainly getting to be whole,” Roberts said Tuesday afternoon.
